title: Accountancy: Numerical Practice and Group C Question Bank

toc.title: 4.1 Bank reconciliation statement from the cash book balance
4.2 Bank reconciliation with an adjusted cash book
4.3 Rectification of errors and the suspense account
4.5 Final accounts with bad debts and a provision

html:
Group C of the Accountancy paper is three questions of eight marks each, and in almost every paper at least one of them is a full numerical — a final-accounts problem, a bank cash book or a statement of expenditure — with a theoretical question offered as its alternative. Group B, too, regularly carries a bank reconciliation statement or a set of rectifying entries. This chapter is therefore a drill book: ten numericals of the kinds that actually appear, each worked out step by step with the table the examiner expects, followed by four Group C theoretical questions with answer outlines.

How to use this chapter

Work each numerical against the clock — a Group C numerical should take about twenty minutes — and only then read the solution. Mark every line you got wrong on a single sheet. In the exam, the marks for a numerical are awarded for the table, the starting figure, the treatment of each item and the arithmetic, in that order: a correct method with one arithmetic slip still earns most of the marks. Each numerical is an original practice question.

4.1 Bank reconciliation statement from the cash book balance

Problem. The cash book of Sagarmatha Traders showed a bank balance of Rs. 84,000 on 30 Chaitra. On comparing it with the passbook the following differences were found. i. Cheques of Rs. 22,000 were issued but not presented for payment. ii. Cheques of Rs. 14,000 were deposited but not yet collected by the bank. iii. Bank charges of Rs. 1,200 had been debited by the bank only. iv. Interest on investment of Rs. 8,000 had been collected by the bank and appeared only in the passbook. v. A customer had deposited Rs. 12,000 directly into the bank, not recorded in the cash book. vi. A cheque of Rs. 6,000 deposited earlier had been dishonoured.

Required. Prepare the bank reconciliation statement.

Solution

Step 1 — Start with the cash book balance: Rs. 84,000. Step 2 — Add the items that make the bank's record higher than the trader's: cheques issued but not presented (Rs. 22,000), interest collected by the bank (Rs. 8,000), direct deposit by a customer (Rs. 12,000). Step 3 — Less the items that make the bank's record lower: cheques deposited but not collected (Rs. 14,000), bank charges (Rs. 1,200), cheque dishonoured (Rs. 6,000).

Particulars Rs. Rs.
Balance as per cash book 84,000
Add: cheques issued but not presented for payment 22,000
Add: interest on investment collected by the bank 8,000
Add: amount deposited directly by a customer 12,000 42,000
1,26,000
Less: cheques deposited but not yet collected 14,000
Less: bank charges debited by the bank 1,200
Less: cheque deposited but dishonoured 6,000 21,200
Balance as per passbook 1,04,800

Answer. Balance as per passbook Rs. 1,04,800.

4.2 Bank reconciliation with an adjusted cash book

Problem. On 31 Ashad the cash book of Himal Traders showed a bank balance of Rs. 42,000. On comparison with the passbook the following were found. i. The cash book showed a payment of Rs. 9,000 for insurance, but the bank had paid Rs. 10,000 on a standing instruction. ii. Bank charges of Rs. 600 and interest on overdraft of Rs. 900 had been debited by the bank only. iii. A customer had deposited Rs. 7,500 directly into the bank. iv. A cheque of Rs. 4,000 deposited earlier had been dishonoured. v. Cheques of Rs. 18,000 issued had not been presented; cheques of Rs. 9,000 deposited had not been collected.

Required. Prepare the adjusted cash book and the bank reconciliation statement.

Solution

Step 1 — Items appearing only in the passbook adjust the cash book: the extra Rs. 1,000 of insurance paid, the bank charges, the interest on overdraft, the customer's direct deposit and the dishonoured cheque. Step 2 — Items that are timing differences stay in the reconciliation: cheques issued but not presented and cheques deposited but not collected.

Adjusted cash book (bank column)

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Balance b/d 42,000 By Insurance (additional paid by bank) 1,000
To Customer's direct deposit 7,500 By Bank charges 600
By Interest on overdraft 900
By Cheque dishonoured 4,000
By Balance c/d (adjusted) 43,000
Total 49,500 Total 49,500

Step 3 — Adjusted balance = 49{,}500 - 6{,}500 = Rs.\ 43{,}000. Step 4 — Reconcile to the passbook.

Bank reconciliation statement as on 31 Ashad

Particulars Rs. Rs.
Balance as per adjusted cash book 43,000
Add: cheques issued but not presented 18,000
61,000
Less: cheques deposited but not collected 9,000
Balance as per passbook 52,000

Answer. Adjusted cash book Rs. 43,000; balance as per passbook Rs. 52,000.

4.3 Rectification of errors and the suspense account

Problem. The following errors were discovered after the trial balance had been prepared. i. Salary paid Rs. 20,000 was wrongly debited to the house rent account. ii. The sales book was overcast by Rs. 5,000. iii. A purchase of machinery of Rs. 40,000 was debited to the purchases account. iv. A sale of Rs. 7,000 to Bina was posted to Bina's account as Rs. 700. v. Wages paid Rs. 3,000 for the erection of a machine were debited to the wages account.

Required. Pass the rectifying entries, state the effect on the trial balance and prepare the suspense account.

Solution

Step 1 — (i) Two expense accounts, both amounts equal: Salary A/c Dr. 20,000; To House Rent A/c 20,000. Two-sided — the trial balance agreed. Step 2 — (ii) The sales book overcast means the credit side is too high: Sales A/c Dr. 5,000; To Suspense A/c 5,000. One-sided — the suspense account was credited with the difference. Step 3 — (iii) An error of principle: Machinery A/c Dr. 40,000; To Purchases A/c 40,000. Two-sided — the trial balance agreed, but profit is understated by Rs. 40,000 and machinery is understated. Step 4 — (iv) Bina's account was debited Rs. 700 instead of Rs. 7,000, short by Rs. 6,300: Bina A/c Dr. 6,300; To Suspense A/c 6,300. One-sided. Step 5 — (v) An error of principle: Machinery A/c Dr. 3,000; To Wages A/c 3,000. Two-sided.

Suspense account

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Balance b/d (if any) — By Sales A/c (overcast) 5,000
By Bina A/c (short posting) 6,300
Total 11,300 Total 11,300

Answer. The debit column of the trial balance was short by Rs. 11,300, carried in the credit of the suspense account and now cleared by the two one-sided corrections. The three two-sided errors (i), (iii) and (v) did not affect the trial balance at all.

4.4 Full final accounts with adjustments

Problem. The following is the trial balance of Sagarmatha Traders as on 31 Ashad 2082.

Particulars Debit (Rs.) Credit (Rs.)
Opening stock 60,000
Purchases 2,40,000
Carriage inward 12,000
Wages 36,000
Salaries 30,000
Rent 20,000
Furniture 80,000
Debtors 55,000
Bank 42,000
Cash 5,000
Capital 1,50,000
Sales 3,50,000
Creditors 50,000
Commission received 30,000
Total 5,80,000 5,80,000

Additional information: (i) closing stock Rs. 70,000; (ii) outstanding salary Rs. 4,000; (iii) prepaid rent Rs. 2,000; (iv) depreciation on furniture at 10 per cent.

Required. Prepare the trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet.

Solution

Step 1 — Cost of goods sold = 60{,}000 + 2{,}40{,}000 + 12{,}000 + 36{,}000 - 70{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}78{,}000; gross profit = 3{,}50{,}000 - 2{,}78{,}000 = Rs.\ 72{,}000.

Trading account for the year ended 31 Ashad 2082

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Opening stock 60,000 By Sales 3,50,000
To Purchases 2,40,000 By Closing stock 70,000
To Carriage inward 12,000
To Wages 36,000
To Gross profit c/d 72,000
Total 4,20,000 Total 4,20,000

Step 2 — Salary becomes 30{,}000 + 4{,}000 = Rs.\ 34{,}000; rent becomes 20{,}000 - 2{,}000 = Rs.\ 18{,}000; depreciation = 10\% \times 80{,}000 = Rs.\ 8{,}000.

Profit and loss account for the year ended 31 Ashad 2082

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Salaries 30,000 By Gross profit b/d 72,000
Add: outstanding salary 4,000 By Commission received 30,000
34,000
To Rent 20,000
Less: prepaid rent 2,000
18,000
To Depreciation on furniture 8,000
To Net profit (transferred to capital) 42,000
Total 1,02,000 Total 1,02,000

Step 3 — Capital = 1{,}50{,}000 + 42{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}92{,}000; furniture = 80{,}000 - 8{,}000 = Rs.\ 72{,}000.

Balance sheet as on 31 Ashad 2082

Liabilities Rs. Assets Rs.
Capital 1,50,000 Furniture 80,000
Add: Net profit 42,000 Less: Depreciation 8,000
1,92,000 72,000
Creditors 50,000 Closing stock 70,000
Outstanding salary 4,000 Debtors 55,000
Bank 42,000
Cash 5,000
Prepaid rent 2,000
Total 2,46,000 Total 2,46,000

Answer. Gross profit Rs. 72,000; net profit Rs. 42,000; balance sheet total Rs. 2,46,000.

4.5 Final accounts with bad debts and a provision

Problem. The trial balance of Himal Traders as on 31 Chaitra 2082 is given below.

Particulars Debit (Rs.) Credit (Rs.)
Opening stock 40,000
Purchases 1,60,000
Wages 20,000
Salaries 24,000
Rent 12,000
Debtors 50,000
Machinery 60,000
Bank 30,000
Cash 4,000
Capital 1,20,000
Sales 2,30,000
Creditors 30,000
Discount received 20,000
Total 4,00,000 4,00,000

Additional information: (i) closing stock Rs. 50,000; (ii) write off bad debts Rs. 2,000; (iii) create a provision for doubtful debts at 5 per cent on the remaining debtors; (iv) depreciate machinery at 10 per cent.

Solution

Step 1 — Cost of goods sold = 40{,}000 + 1{,}60{,}000 + 20{,}000 - 50{,}000 = Rs.\ 1{,}70{,}000; gross profit = 2{,}30{,}000 - 1{,}70{,}000 = Rs.\ 60{,}000. Step 2 — Debtors after bad debts = 50{,}000 - 2{,}000 = Rs.\ 48{,}000; provision = 5\% \times 48{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}400; depreciation = 10\% \times 60{,}000 = Rs.\ 6{,}000.

Trading account for the year ended 31 Chaitra 2082

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Opening stock 40,000 By Sales 2,30,000
To Purchases 1,60,000 By Closing stock 50,000
To Wages 20,000
To Gross profit c/d 60,000
Total 2,80,000 Total 2,80,000

Profit and loss account for the year ended 31 Chaitra 2082

Particulars Rs. Particulars Rs.
To Salaries 24,000 By Gross profit b/d 60,000
To Rent 12,000 By Discount received 20,000
To Bad debts 2,000

To Depreciation on machinery 6,000

Balance sheet as on 31 Chaitra 2082

Add: Net profit 33,600 Less: Depreciation 6,000
1,53,600 54,000

Debtors 50,000

48,000

45,600

Answer. Gross profit Rs. 60,000; net profit Rs. 33,600; balance sheet total Rs. 1,83,600.

4.6 Bank cash book (A.G.F. No. 209)

Problem. The following transactions took place in the bank account of a District Coordination Unit during the month of Shrawan 2082. There was no opening balance. i. 04/02 — budget release received from the Treasury and Comptroller Office, Rs. 6,00,000. ii. 04/08 — payment order issued against 22311 office materials, Rs. 45,000. iii. 04/12 — advance of Rs. 70,000 given to a section officer against 31111 for the purchase of a computer. iv. 04/20 — the advance was cleared on a bill of Rs. 82,000, the excess being paid by payment order. v. 04/25 — salary payment order for the month, total salary Rs. 2,40,000, after deducting provident fund Rs. 30,000 and income tax Rs. 5,000. vi. 04/28 — the provident fund and income tax deducted were deposited.

Required. Prepare the bank cash book and state the closing balance.

Solution

Step 1 — The release is money received: debit Rs. 6,00,000. Step 2 — Office materials Rs. 45,000 and the advance Rs. 70,000 are payments: credits. Step 3 — On clearance, only the excess of Rs. 82,000 − Rs. 70,000 = Rs. 12,000 is a fresh payment; the rest clears the advance. Step 4 — Salary: only the net Rs. 2,40,000 − 30,000 − 5,000 = Rs. 2,05,000 leaves the bank. Step 5 — The deductions deposited, Rs. 35,000, also leave the bank.

Date Voucher no. Particulars Debit (Rs.) Credit (Rs.) Balance (Rs.)
04/02 1 Budget release received from the DTCO 6,00,000 6,00,000
04/08 2 Payment order — 22311 office materials 45,000 5,55,000
04/12 3 Advance to section officer — 31111 computer 70,000 4,85,000
04/20 4 Excess of the computer bill over the advance (82,000 − 70,000) 12,000 4,73,000
04/25 5 Salary of Shrawan, net of provident fund Rs. 30,000 and income tax Rs. 5,000 2,05,000 2,68,000
04/28 6 Provident fund and income tax deposited 35,000 2,33,000
04/30 Balance c/d 2,33,000 —
Total 6,00,000 6,00,000

Answer. Total receipts Rs. 6,00,000; total payments Rs. 3,67,000; closing balance Rs. 2,33,000 (debit), subject to reconciliation with the passbook. Note that the computer head 31111 finally carries Rs. 82,000 of expenditure, while only Rs. 12,000 of it was paid after the advance.

4.7 Statement of expenditure

Problem. The following particulars relate to a District Office for the month of Poush 2082.

Head no. Head Annual appropriation (Rs.) Expenditure up to Poush (Rs.) Expenditure of Poush (Rs.)
21111 Remuneration 5,00,000 2,10,000 35,000
22111 Uniform 60,000 9,000 1,500
22311 Office materials 25,000 12,000 2,000
22612 Travelling expenses 90,000 34,000 8,000
22711 Miscellaneous expenses 45,000 13,000 2,500

An uncleared advance of Rs. 6,000 for fuel is outstanding.

Required. Prepare the statement of expenditure showing the available balance.

Solution

Step 1 — Total appropriation = 5{,}00{,}000 + 60{,}000 + 25{,}000 + 90{,}000 + 45{,}000 = Rs.\ 7{,}20{,}000. Step 2 — Total expenditure up to Poush = 2{,}10{,}000 + 9{,}000 + 12{,}000 + 34{,}000 + 13{,}000 = Rs.\ 2{,}78{,}000. Step 3 — Total expenditure of Poush = 35{,}000 + 1{,}500 + 2{,}000 + 8{,}000 + 2{,}500 = Rs.\ 49{,}000. Step 4 — Available balance = 7{,}20{,}000 - 2{,}78{,}000 - 6{,}000 = Rs.\ 4{,}36{,}000.

Head no. Head Appropriation (Rs.) Expenditure to date (Rs.) Of Poush (Rs.) Uncleared advance (Rs.) Available (Rs.)
21111 Remuneration 5,00,000 2,10,000 35,000 — 2,90,000
22111 Uniform 60,000 9,000 1,500 — 51,000
22311 Office materials 25,000 12,000 2,000 — 13,000
22612 Travelling expenses 90,000 34,000 8,000 6,000 50,000
22711 Miscellaneous 45,000 13,000 2,500 — 32,000
Total 7,20,000 2,78,000 49,000 6,000 4,36,000

Answer. Appropriation Rs. 7,20,000; expenditure to date Rs. 2,78,000; Poush expenditure Rs. 49,000; uncleared advance Rs. 6,000; available balance Rs. 4,36,000.

4.8 Government journal vouchers

Problem. Pass the journal vouchers for the following transactions of a District Administration Office. i. A payment order of Rs. 70,000 was issued against budget head 31111 for the purchase of a computer. ii. An advance of Rs. 90,000 was given to a section officer against 31121 for the purchase of furniture. iii. The advance was cleared on a furniture bill of Rs. 1,05,000, the excess being paid by a further payment order. iv. Provident fund of Rs. 25,000 and income tax of Rs. 3,000 deducted from the salary of the month were deposited into the concerned office.

Solution

Step 1 — (i) 31111 Machinery and equipment (computer) A/c Dr. 70,000; To DTCO A/c 70,000. (Being a payment order issued for the purchase of a computer.) Step 2 — (ii) Furniture advance A/c Dr. 90,000; To DTCO A/c 90,000. (Being an advance issued for the purchase of furniture.) Step 3 — (iii) 31121 Furniture and fixtures A/c Dr. 1,05,000; To Furniture advance A/c 90,000; To DTCO A/c 15,000. (Being the furniture advance cleared on a bill of Rs. 1,05,000, the excess of Rs. 15,000 being payable.) Step 4 — (iv) Provident fund payable A/c Dr. 25,000; Income tax payable A/c Dr. 3,000; To Bank A/c 28,000. (Being the amount deducted from salary deposited into the concerned office.) Answer. The four vouchers above. Note that (ii) is not an expenditure but a recoverable advance, and that the furniture head finally carries Rs. 1,05,000.

4.9 Retention accounting

Problem. A contractor's running bill for a road contract is Rs. 6,00,000. A retention of 5 per cent is withheld. Later, a defect costing Rs. 18,000 is not remedied by the contractor. Show the journal vouchers (a) when the bill is passed, (b) when the retention is released in full if no defect appears, and (c) when the retention is adjusted and the balance forfeited.

Solution

Step 1 — Retention = 5\% \times 6{,}00{,}000 = Rs.\ 30{,}000; net paid = Rs.\ 5{,}70{,}000. Step 2 — (a) Road construction expenditure A/c Dr. 6,00,000; To Contractors' retention A/c 30,000; To Bank / DTCO A/c 5,70,000. (Being the running bill passed and retention of 5 per cent withheld.) Step 3 — (b) Contractors' retention A/c Dr. 30,000; To Bank A/c 30,000. (Being the retention released on the expiry of the defect liability period.) Step 4 — (c) Contractors' retention A/c Dr. 30,000; To Repair and maintenance expenditure A/c 18,000; To Miscellaneous revenue A/c 12,000. (Being the retention adjusted against the cost of remedying the defect and the balance forfeited to government revenue.) Answer. Retention Rs. 30,000 in each case; on forfeiture Rs. 18,000 is set against the repair expenditure and Rs. 12,000 becomes revenue. Until it is released or forfeited, the retention is a liability, not revenue.

4.10 Revenue statement

Problem. A District Education Office collected the following revenue up to the month of Poush. Prepare the revenue statement and state the amount to be deposited.

Head Description Collected (Rs.) Undeposited (Rs.)
14223 Income from the education sector 3,60,000 —
14224 Examination fee 2,40,000 40,000
14227 Passport fee 1,20,000 20,000
14151 Rent of government property 1,80,000 —
Solution

Step 1 — Total collected = 3{,}60{,}000 + 2{,}40{,}000 + 1{,}20{,}000 + 1{,}80{,}000 = Rs.\ 9{,}00{,}000. Step 2 — Total undeposited = 40{,}000 + 20{,}000 = Rs.\ 60{,}000. Step 3 — Deposited in the period = 9{,}00{,}000 - 60{,}000 = Rs.\ 8{,}40{,}000.

Head code Description Collected (Rs.) Deposited (Rs.) Cash in hand (Rs.)
14151 Rent of government property 1,80,000 1,80,000 —
14223 Income from the education sector 3,60,000 3,60,000 —
14224 Examination fee 2,40,000 2,00,000 40,000
14227 Passport fee 1,20,000 1,00,000 20,000
Total 9,00,000 8,40,000 60,000

Check: 9{,}00{,}000 = 8{,}40{,}000 + 60{,}000. ✔ Answer. Collected Rs. 9,00,000; deposited Rs. 8,40,000; Rs. 60,000 to be deposited on the first working day of the next month.

4.11 VAT chain

Problem. A producer sells goods to a wholesaler for Rs. 3,00,000, the wholesaler sells them to a retailer for Rs. 3,60,000 and the retailer sells them to the consumer for Rs. 4,00,000, all prices being exclusive of VAT. The VAT rate is 13 per cent. Compute the VAT deposited by each dealer and the total received by the government, and verify the total.

Solution
Stage Sale price (Rs.) Value added (Rs.) Output tax (Rs.) Input tax (Rs.) Deposited (Rs.)
Producer 3,00,000 3,00,000 39,000 — 39,000
Wholesaler 3,60,000 60,000 46,800 39,000 7,800
Retailer 4,00,000 40,000 52,000 46,800 5,200
Total 4,00,000 52,000

Step 1 — Producer: 13\% \times 3{,}00{,}000 = 39{,}000. Step 2 — Wholesaler: output 13\% \times 3{,}60{,}000 = 46{,}800; less input 39,000 → 7,800. Step 3 — Retailer: output 13\% \times 4{,}00{,}000 = 52{,}000; less input 46,800 → 5,200. Step 4 — Verification: 39{,}000 + 7{,}800 + 5{,}200 = 52{,}000 = 13\% \times 4{,}00{,}000. ✔ Answer. Producer Rs. 39,000; wholesaler Rs. 7,800; retailer Rs. 5,200; total Rs. 52,000, borne entirely by the final consumer.

4.12 Store ledger

Problem. The store of a government office holds steel chairs under head 31121. On Baisakh 1, 60 chairs were received at Rs. 2,800 each. On Baisakh 6, 15 chairs were issued to the administration section; on Baisakh 15, 30 more were received; on Baisakh 24, 20 were issued to the examination section. Complete the store ledger and find the value of the closing stock.

Solution
Date Particulars Receipt (no.) Issue (no.) Balance (no.)
Baisakh 1 Received from the supplier 60 60
Baisakh 6 Issued to the administration section 15 45
Baisakh 15 Received from the supplier 30 75
Baisakh 24 Issued to the examination section 20 55

Step 1 — Total received = 60 + 30 = 90; total issued = 15 + 20 = 35; balance = 55. Step 2 — Closing stock = 55 \times 2{,}800 = Rs.\ 1{,}54{,}000. Answer. Closing balance 55 chairs, valued at Rs. 1,54,000. The bin card on the shelf must show exactly the same three numbers.

4.13 Group C theoretical questions

  1. What is a bank reconciliation statement? Explain its need and the causes that make the cash book and the passbook differ, and show the usual format starting from the cash book balance. [8]
  2. What is an accounting error? Explain the types of errors and state which of them are detected by the trial balance and which are not. [8]
  3. What are final accounts? Explain the steps in their preparation and the treatment of any five adjustments, stating in each case the two effects. [8]
  4. What is a bank cash book? Explain its columns and the rules for its preparation, and state which items are entered on the debit side and which on the credit side. [8]
Answer outlines

1. Definition (1). A statement prepared on a date to explain and reconcile the difference between the bank column of the cash book and the passbook. Need (3). To check the accuracy of both records and trace errors; to find the true bank balance; to detect dishonoured cheques, unrecorded charges and direct deposits; to prepare the balance sheet; to prevent fraud; to satisfy the auditor and the bank. Causes (2). Timing — cheques issued but not presented, cheques deposited but not collected. Bank-only entries — bank charges, interest, dividend collected, direct deposits, standing instructions, dishonoured cheques. Errors in either book. Format (2). Start with the cash book balance; add cheques issued but not presented, interest and dividends collected, direct deposits and wrong credits by the bank; less cheques deposited but not collected, bank charges and interest on overdraft, dishonoured cheques, standing instructions and wrong debits; arrive at the passbook balance. Show the table.

2. Definition (1). A mistake in recording, posting, casting, carrying forward or summarising a transaction, or in applying an accounting principle. Types (4). Errors of principle (capital expenditure treated as revenue and the reverse); errors of omission (complete and partial); errors of commission (wrong amount, wrong account, wrong side, wrong casting, wrong balance carried forward); compensating errors. Explain each with an example. Detection (3). The trial balance detects only one-sided errors — casting and balancing errors, posting to the wrong side, a wrong amount posted in one account, partial omission. It cannot detect two-sided errors — errors of principle, complete omission, compensating errors, the wrong account of the same class and a transaction entered twice in both accounts. Conclude that the trial balance proves arithmetical accuracy only.

3. Definition (1). The statements prepared at the end of the period from the trial balance after adjustments, to show the profit or loss and the financial position. Steps (3). Complete and agree the trial balance; bring in the closing entries; prepare the trading account and find the gross profit; prepare the profit and loss account and find the net profit; add the net profit to capital and deduct drawings; prepare the balance sheet; check that the two sides agree. Adjustments (4). Explain any five out of: closing stock, outstanding expense, prepaid expense, accrued income, income received in advance, depreciation, interest on capital, interest on drawings, goods taken by the proprietor, provision for doubtful debts, manager's commission — stating in each case the effect in the trading or profit and loss account and the effect in the balance sheet. Emphasise that every adjustment has two effects, and that a missing second effect is the commonest reason for a balance sheet not tallying.

4. Meaning (2). The bank cash book, म.ले.प.फा.नं. २०९, is the operating level office's combined record of its bank account, showing all money received and paid with a running balance. Columns (2). Date; voucher number; particulars; debit (money received); credit (money paid); balance. Debit side (2). Budget release received, revenue deposited, retention and deductions received, refund of an unspent advance, amount transferred in. Credit side (2). Expenditure paid, advances paid, retention and deductions paid over or refunded, amounts transferred out, and the closing balance carried down. Add the rules: enter in date order with the voucher number; carry a running balance; total both sides; reconcile with the passbook every month and send a copy with the statement of expenditure.
